claims.claim: Honey found in ancient Egyptian tombs — roughly 3,000 years old — has been reported in edible condition by archaeologists.
claims.definition: honey stored in sealed ceramic vessels in tombs, found unspoiled after ~3,000 years
claims.authoritative_source: Smithsonian Magazine — 'The Science Behind Honey's Eternal Shelf Life'
claims.notes: status stable; recurring archaeology report, not a living record

claims.claim: Microbial growth requires available water: most spoilage bacteria cannot grow below a water activity of about 0.91.
claims.definition: water activity (aw) minimum for bacterial growth
claims.authoritative_source: FDA Bad Bug Book (2nd edition), microbial growth parameters

claims.claim: Honey is a supersaturated sugar solution (~82% sugars, ~17-18% water); its high osmotic pressure draws water out of microbial cells, inhibiting growth.
claims.authoritative_source: National Honey Board — honey composition and stability
claims.notes: mechanism statement consistent with food-microbiology literature

claims.claim: Nectar commonly runs 60-80% water; bees reduce it to honey at 17-18% water before capping the cells.
claims.definition: water content of nectar vs finished honey
claims.authoritative_source: USDA Agricultural Research Service — honey processing
claims.notes: ranges vary by floral source; figures are standard

claims.claim: Honeybees evaporate nectar by fanning with rapid wingbeats — about 230 beats per second — speeding the water loss that turns nectar into honey.
claims.definition: fanning behavior and honeybee wingbeat frequency
claims.authoritative_source: USDA-ARS Carl Hayden Bee Research Center; insect-flight literature
claims.notes: wingbeat ≈230 Hz is the standard measured figure for Apis mellifera

claims.claim: Honey is acidic, with a pH typically between 3.2 and 4.5, due mainly to gluconic acid.
claims.authoritative_source: Bogdanov, S. — Bee Product Science, honey composition reviews

claims.claim: Bees add the enzyme glucose oxidase to nectar; in honey it slowly generates trace hydrogen peroxide, one of honey's antibacterial systems.
claims.authoritative_source: Molan, P.C. — reviews of honey's antibacterial activity (Univ. of Waikato)
claims.notes: well-established mechanism in apitherapy research literature
